title: Effects of 120 vs. 60 and 90 g/h Carbohydrate Intake during a Trail Marathon on Neuromuscular Function and High Intensity Run Capacity Recovery
authors: Urdampilleta A, Arribalzaga S, Viribay A, Castaneda-Babarro A, Seco-Calvo J, Mielgo-Ayuso J
population: 26 elite trail runners, 4000 m cumulative-slope mountain marathon
findings: Randomised to LOW (60 g/h), MED (90 g/h) or HIGH (120 g/h) CHO intake.
Abalakov jump time/height and half-squat 1RM changed significantly 24 h post-race in LOW and MED but not HIGH (Wilcoxon).

Internal load significantly lower in HIGH vs LOW and MED (p = 0.017); changes in jump (p = 0.038), half-squat (p = 0.041), fatigue (p = 0.018) and lactate (p = 0.012) in the aerobic power-capacity test were smaller in HIGH.
Authors conclude 120 g/h might limit neuromuscular fatigue and improve recovery of high-intensity run capacity 24 h after the race.
limitations: About 8-9 per arm, non-parametric tests, recovery measures only at 24 h, no race performance or GI outcomes in the abstract; study motivated by the authors' prior work on 120 g/h.
implications: Evidence for > 90 g/h in running is preliminary: allow 90-120 g/h only as an advanced athlete opt-in tier for athletes already tolerating 90 g/h, flagged low-certainty.

verification.notes: Crossref match; numbers from the Europe PMC abstract. Removed unverified commercial-link and '~4-5 h' claims.
